name: Ahi
title: Head of a family in the tribe of Gad, son of Abdiel
summary: Ahi is known from the genealogy of the tribe of Gad in 1 Chronicles, where he is listed as the son of Abdiel and grandson of Guni. He served as a family head among the Gadites, who lived in Gilead and Bashan—the fertile lands east of the Jordan River. According to the text, this genealogy was recorded during the overlapping reigns of Jotham, king of Judah, and Jeroboam II, king of Israel, dating it to the mid-700s BC. Although Ahi is mentioned only briefly, his placement in the record attests to a prominent position within the tribe's leadership structure. The context surrounding this entry also sheds light on the geographic spread of the Gadites in Transjordan, an area that would soon be lost to the Assyrian empire.

keyEvents.title: Listed in the genealogy of Gad
keyEvents.description: Ahi is mentioned as the son of Abdiel, son of Guni, and listed among the heads of families in the tribe of Gad in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles.

keyEvents.title: Settlement of the Gadites in Gilead and Bashan
keyEvents.description: The tribe of Gad, to which Ahi belonged, lived in the land of Gilead and in Bashan with its associated cities, as well as on the pastures of Sharon as far as they extended. This description highlights the tribe's connection to the fertile regions east of the Jordan.

keyEvents.title: Genealogical registration during Jotham and Jeroboam II
keyEvents.description: The genealogy of Gad, which included Ahi, was recorded during the overlapping reigns of Judah's king Jotham and Israel's king Jeroboam II, dating the registration to approximately the 8th century BC.

versions.reason: [minor] The title is correct but could have been slightly more informative by mentioning that he was a family head; [major] The role 'leader' is somewhat imprecise. 1 Chr 5:15 describes Ahi as 'head of his father's house' (rosh bet avotam). A more appropriate role would be 'family head' or 'tribal member'. It is not clear that he was a 'leader' in the broader sense; [minor] The last two events (verses 16–18) concern the tribe of Gad generally, not specifically Ahi. It is acceptable to include them as context, but the descriptions should clarify that this is general information about the tribe; [minor] Footnotes are missing. Notes should be added regarding the meaning of the name Ahi, the geographical location of Gilead, and the context for the genealogies in 1 Chronicles.

versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 and should be rephrased to provide a fresher presentation. It begins with almost identical wording ('Ahi is a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles who belonged to the tribe of Gad').; [minor] The explanation 'brother of the Lord' for Ahijah is misleading. Ahijah (אֲחִיָּה) more accurately means 'my brother is YHWH' or 'YHWH is a brother', not 'the Lord's brother'. This should be corrected.; [minor] The role 'tribesman' is very generic and provides little information. A more precise role such as 'Gadite' or similar could be considered.; [minor] Verse 16 specifically mentions the settlement, but Ahi himself is explicitly mentioned only in verse 15. The event is contextual and relevant, but the description should clarify that this applies to the tribe generally, not to Ahi specifically.

versions.summary: In the genealogy of Gad's tribe in 1 Chronicles, Ahi appears as a family head among the Gadites. He was the son of Abdiel and grandson of Guni, belonging to that part of Gad's tribe which settled in Gilead and Bashan, the fertile regions east of the Jordan. The genealogy listing him was recorded during the reigns of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam II king of Israel, linking him to the period of the divided kingdom in the 700s BC. Although little is known about his individual deeds, his place in the genealogy testifies to his significance as a leader within his clan and tribe.

versions.reason: [major] The summary states that the genealogy was recorded 'in the 700s BC' but at the same time mentions Jeroboam II (who reigned c. 793–753 BC) and Jotham (c. 750–735 BC). The overlapping period is approximately 750–753 BC. Furthermore, it states that the registration took place 'during the reign of Judah's king Jotham and Israel's king Jeroboam II', but the summary uses 'the 700s BC' which is slightly imprecise but acceptable. However, lifespan says 'c. the 800s BC' while the summary says 'the 700s BC' - this is contradictory.; [major] Lifespan is set to 'c. the 800s BC' but the genealogical registration is dated to the reigns of Jotham and Jeroboam II, which overlap around 750–753 BC. If Ahi lived when the registration was made, his lifespan should be placed closer to the middle of the 700s BC, not the 800s.; [minor] Since there are two earlier versions with similar text, the summary should be rephrased further to avoid similarity with previous versions and provide a more unique and engaging presentation.; [minor] The linguistic footnote uses the term 'teofart' - this is a typo for 'theophoric'.; [minor] The second key event ('Gad's tribe in Gilead and Bashan') is actually not an event specifically linked to Ahi, but a general description of the tribe's dwelling place. It is nevertheless contextually relevant and acceptable given the limited information about Ahi.

footnotes.text: The name Ahi (אֲחִי) probably means 'my brother' in Hebrew. Some scholars view it as a shortened form of a theophoric name like Ahijah (אֲחִיָּה), which could mean 'my brother is YHWH'. Others believe it is simply a kinship-based name expressing family belonging.

Gilead and Bashan were regions east of the Jordan River traditionally assigned to the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh. Gilead was known for its fertile grazing lands, balsam cultivation, and forested highlands, and is frequently mentioned in the Old Testament.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 5 state that the recording took place under Jotham, king of Judah (c. 750–735 BC), and Jeroboam II, king of Israel (c. 793–753 BC). The overlapping period between these two kings places the recording around 750–753 BC.

The pasturelands of Sharon in 1 Chron 5:16 likely do not refer to the well-known Sharon plain on the Mediterranean coast, but rather to a grazing area with the same name in Transjordan. This interpretation is supported by the context, which deals exclusively with lands east of the Jordan.

The genealogies in Chronicles served an important function after the Babylonian exile by connecting the returned people to their tribal identity and the ancient land promises. For the Gadites, this was especially relevant since their territories in Transjordan were lost already during the Assyrian expansion in the 8th century BC (cf. 2 Kgs 15:29).
